items.title: DNA methylation patterns at the IGF2-H19 locus in offspring and maternal folate intake: a systematic review.
items.venue: Journal of developmental origins of health and disease

ai.headline: Maternal folic acid in pregnancy is linked to small, region-specific changes in offspring DNA methylation at the IGF2-H19 locus.
ai.summary: This systematic review examined human studies on maternal folate or folic acid intake during pregnancy and DNA methylation at the IGF2-H19 locus in offspring tissues. Folic acid supplementation showed the most consistent associations at the H19 imprinting control region, with some cord blood analyses reporting inverse associations with methylation, while IGF2 DMR2 results varied and dietary folate intake was largely null.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how a common pregnancy supplement may be linked to molecular changes in a developing baby, though the real-world importance remains unclear.
ai.life_skill: Talk to a qualified healthcare professional about folic acid supplementation during pregnancy.
ai.fact: Folate is a critical methyl-group donor in one-carbon metabolism.
ai.caveat: No observational study was at low overall risk of bias, both trials had some concerns, and findings were heterogeneous, so firm conclusions about biological significance cannot be drawn.

ai.summary: The paper reviews laboratory, animal and human studies on oral collagen peptides. items.title: Effectiveness of nurse-led hypertension interventions on retention, adherence, and blood pressure control among adults in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review

ai.headline: Nurse-led care may improve blood pressure control in low- and middle-income countries, but retention results varied widely.
ai.summary: This systematic review looked at 11 studies involving 19,005 adults with hypertension in primary care clinics across Africa and Asia. Most studies found nurse-led interventions reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure, while retention rates and medication adherence showed mixed or limited results.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how non-doctor health workers can help manage a common condition in places with limited medical staff, which matters for everyday health and global health planning.
ai.life_skill: If you have high blood pressure, ask a qualified health professional whether nurse-led support or regular follow-up could help you stay on track with care.
ai.fact: Hypertension affects more than 1.28 billion adults globally and is a leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke, kidney failure and premature death.

quiz.question: What did most studies report about blood pressure after nurse-led interventions?
quiz.answer: Most studies reported a reduction in systolic blood pressure greater than 10 mmHg and a reduction in diastolic blood pressure.

ai.caveat: The studies varied widely in design and quality, many had high or unclear risk of bias due to missing data, and blood pressure reductions were within-group estimates rather than a pooled effect.

items.title: Testing implications of the network theory of mental disorders in intensive short-term treatment

ai.headline: Intensive therapy reduced depression and anxiety symptoms but did not substantially weaken how those symptoms interact with each other.
ai.summary: Researchers analysed data from 288 adults receiving seven weeks of intensive inpatient or day-clinic treatment for moderate to severe depression. Symptom severity fell, but only three of 36 symptom-to-symptom links changed much, and overall symptom connectivity barely dropped.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and it is a secondary analysis of one trial in Germany, so the results are not yet confirmed.

ai.fact: Some clinical uncertainty is ambiguity where the degree of uncertainty may not be known or straightforward to communicate.

quiz.answer: Ambiguity caused by missing, imprecise, or conflicting information.

items.title: Computation, not weight access: large language models as auditors of clinical prediction networks

ai.headline: AI can audit small medical prediction networks by running calculations, even without seeing their internal weights.
ai.summary: Researchers tested whether large language models could audit small neural networks trained on simulated patient data for subarachnoid haemorrhage. ai.fact: Sleep quality and microsleep tendencies are linked to academic performance in aviation vocational students.

quiz.question: Which behaviour was the strongest predictor of better sleep quality in the study?

items.title: Students’ intentions to truthfully declare generative AI use in higher education assessment: a cross-sectional SEM study integrating deterrence theory and the theory of planned behavior

ai.headline: Students’ intentions to honestly declare AI use depend on attitudes, social pressure, and how detection and penalties are framed.
ai.summary: A cross-sectional survey of 466 Chinese university students examined what influences intentions to truthfully declare generative AI use in assessments. Positive attitudes, social norms, and perceived control were linked to stronger intentions. Detection certainty for non-disclosure and sanction severity for improper use were linked to better attitudes and control, while sanction severity for non-disclosure and identification certainty for improper use were linked to worse attitudes and control.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that how institutions frame AI detection and penalties can shape whether students feel able and willing to be honest about AI use.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether AI rules focus on catching non-disclosure or punishing misuse, since this shapes how honest people feel about declaring use.
ai.fact: Different deterrence targets—catching non-disclosure versus identifying improper use—can have opposite effects on attitudes toward honest AI disclosure.

quiz.question: Which factors were positively linked to students’ intentions to truthfully declare AI use?
quiz.answer: Positive attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control were all positively associated with the intention to truthfully declare generative AI use.

ai.caveat: Because it is a single cross-sectional survey of students in China measuring intentions rather than actual behavior, it cannot prove causation and may not generalise.

items.title: Memory Self-Awareness Phenotypes are Associated with Alzheimers Disease Biomarker Burden and Clinical Progression in Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment

ai.headline: People with mild memory problems who lack awareness of their memory decline may face faster progression toward Alzheimer's disease.
ai.summary: Researchers studied 590 people with mild cognitive impairment and grouped them by how well their own memory ratings matched a friend or family member's ratings. Those unaware of memory problems had more Alzheimer's biomarkers and were more than twice as likely to progress clinically, while the worried well group had lower risk.
ai.why_it_matters: Recognising a gap between how you see your memory and how others see it could help flag the need for professional assessment sooner.
ai.life_skill: Ask a trusted friend or family member how they rate your everyday memory, and compare it with your own rating.
ai.fact: Memory self-awareness can be measured by comparing a person's own memory report with an informant's report.

quiz.question: What did researchers use to identify memory self-awareness phenotypes?
quiz.answer: They compared participants' own memory ratings with ratings from an informant, such as a friend or family member.

ai.caveat: This is a single preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and its observational design cannot prove that unawareness causes faster progression.

items.title: Science Media Centre “legitimises” industries that harm health, study claims

ai.headline: A UK science media centre’s funding from health-harming industries may legitimise their public health roles, researchers say.
ai.summary: Researchers at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and the University of Edinburgh examined the Science Media Centre’s funding, governance, and rapid reactions to science news from 2019. They concluded that its funding model amplifies and legitimises the positions of industries that harm health. The centre’s chief executive said small, no-strings donations protect its editorial independence.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how money from companies linked to poor health can shape the science news that reaches the public through major media outlets.
ai.life_skill: Check who funds a science news organisation before relying on its expert comments.
ai.fact: The Science Media Centre provides expert commentary and press briefings to major UK media outlets on breaking science news.

quiz.question: What did researchers say the Science Media Centre’s funding model does?
quiz.answer: It legitimises health-harming industries as partners in public health endeavours.

ai.caveat: The findings come from a single observational analysis of one organisation’s funding and media output, so they cannot prove that the funding caused media bias.

items.title: Is shorter daylight dragging down your mood? What to know about seasonal affective disorder

ai.headline: Shorter, colder days are linked to low mood known as the winter blues.
ai.summary: The piece describes the “winter blues” as a blah, low-energy feeling that can settle in as days grow shorter, colder and grayer. It does not report a study, participants, or measured results.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps people recognise a common seasonal pattern in mood and energy.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether your mood or energy dips as daylight gets shorter.
ai.fact: Shorter, colder, grayer days are linked to low-energy, low mood sometimes called the winter blues.

quiz.question: What does the phrase “winter blues” describe?
quiz.answer: A blah, low-energy feeling that can settle in as days grow shorter, colder and grayer.

ai.caveat: This is a news report, not a research study, so it provides no data, sample size or proof of cause and effect.

items.title: Value-oriented policy distillation for interpretable wind farm power control

ai.headline: A transparent AI method helped a wind farm cut imbalance costs by 82% in a simulation.
ai.summary: Researchers developed a control system for wind farms that uses explainable AI to adjust power output based on grid prices. In a simulation using real Belgian data, this transparent method reduced imbalance costs by 82% compared to standard approaches.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how making AI decisions transparent can help critical infrastructure like the power grid operate more efficiently and reliably.
ai.fact: Explainable boosting machines can be used to create control policies that are both effective and understandable to humans.

quiz.question: Why did the researchers choose explainable boosting machines for the wind farm controller?
quiz.answer: They were chosen because standard reinforcement learning methods lack the interpretability needed for real-world deployment.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint based on a simulation using historical data, not a peer-reviewed study of real-time grid operations.

items.title: Kinship, acoustic signaling, and socio-spatial structure shape shared decisions and social influence in white-nosed coatis

ai.headline: Coati groups follow the majority, but leaders and relatives have more influence on direction.
ai.summary: Researchers tracked wild white-nosed coati groups to see how they decide where to go. They found that coatis usually follow the majority opinion, but they are more likely to follow closer relatives or individuals positioned at the front of the group.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that group decisions are not just about counting votes; social relationships and physical position also shape who gets to lead.
ai.life_skill: Notice how physical position and social closeness might affect who others follow in a group setting.
ai.fact: In wild coati groups, individuals who consistently formed majorities or occupied frontward positions had higher influence over travel direction.

quiz.question: Besides the majority opinion, what two factors made coatis more likely to follow a specific groupmate?
quiz.answer: Coatis were more likely to follow closer kin and groupmates in more frontward spatial positions.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so the findings are not yet fully validated by the scientific community.

items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years

ai.headline: Scientists found chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones.
ai.summary: Researchers examined dinosaur bones that are 115 million years old and detected chemically confirmed traces of blood. This discovery challenges previous assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive in fossils.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that biological materials can last far longer than expected, which helps us understand ancient life and may guide the search for life on other planets.
ai.fact: Biological molecules like blood can potentially survive for over 100 million years under the right conditions.

quiz.question: How old were the dinosaur bones where the blood traces were found?
quiz.answer: The bones were 115 million years old.

ai.caveat: This is a news report summarising a scientific finding, not a peer-reviewed study itself, so the specific chemical methods and sample sizes are not detailed here.

items.title: A really simple guide to climate change

ai.summary: This BBC News guide explains that human activities are causing global warming, which poses serious risks to people and the natural world.
ai.why_it_matters: Knowing the cause of climate change helps people understand the risks behind extreme weather and environmental news.
ai.life_skill: Try checking reliable sources such as the BBC or scientific organisations when you read about climate change.

quiz.answer: Human activities are causing the world to heat up.

items.title: Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench: The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling

ai.headline: A new computer benchmark tests whether AI agents can solve real-world maths modelling problems and check if answers are physically possible.
ai.summary: Researchers created TB-MathModel, a benchmark using 18 real contest-style maths problems where AI agents work in a terminal and return one JSON answer. The system scores answers against multiple outstanding human papers and uses a hard gate that zeroes answers that are not physically feasible, with top multimodal models reaching 64.58% and an open model reaching 59.81%.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how researchers are building ways to measure whether AI can turn messy real-world problems into workable mathematical solutions, which matters as these tools are used more in everyday decision-making.

quiz.question: What happens to an answer in TB-MathModel if it is not physically feasible?
quiz.answer: A hard gate zeroes infeasible answers.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so its findings are not yet confirmed.

items.title: Rise of Germanic and Celtic languages is written in ancient DNA

ai.headline: Ancient DNA from thousands of genomes suggests migrations may have spread early Germanic and Celtic languages across Europe.
ai.summary: Researchers analysed thousands of genome sequences to trace human movements in Europe. Their findings suggest that migrations could have carried early forms of Germanic and Celtic languages across the continent.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how studying ancient DNA can help us understand how languages and people moved across Europe in the distant past.
ai.fact: Thousands of ancient genome sequences have been used to identify human migrations linked to the spread of early Germanic and Celtic languages.

quiz.question: What did researchers use thousands of genome sequences to identify?
quiz.answer: They used them to identify human migrations that might have spread early forms of Germanic and Celtic languages around Europe.

ai.caveat: The study identifies migrations that might have spread languages, but cannot prove that migration caused the languages to spread.

items.title: Parkinson’s may be driven by ‘vicious cycle’ that disrupts brain waste drainage

ai.headline: Parkinson’s may be driven by a cycle linking toxic protein clumps and poor brain waste drainage
ai.summary: The report discusses Parkinson’s disease, which is linked to toxic protein clumps and disrupted brain waste removal. It suggests these two problems may feed off each other, helping the condition progress.
ai.why_it_matters: It highlights how brain waste clearance could be important in understanding how Parkinson’s develops and worsens over time.
ai.fact: Parkinson’s disease is linked to toxic protein clumps and disrupted brain waste removal.

quiz.question: What may feed off each other in Parkinson’s disease according to the report?
quiz.answer: Toxic protein clumps and disrupted brain waste removal may feed off each other.

items.title: [Correspondence] Global health: dying from failure or fulfilment?

ai.headline: A Lancet editor reflects on whether global health has lost its radical edge and links it to citizen organising in Japan.
ai.summary: Richard Horton writes a letter to The Lancet asking if global health can recover its lost radicalism, referencing Saul Alinsky's Reveille for Radicals. He notes the book was translated into Japanese in 1972, arriving during a period of citizen movements against industrial pollution and other social problems in Japan.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how ideas about citizen participation and power can shape responses to health and social problems in different countries.
ai.life_skill: Notice how community groups organise around local problems and consider whether you could join or support one.
ai.fact: Saul Alinsky's Reveille for Radicals was translated into Japanese and published in 1972.

quiz.question: What does Richard Horton ask about global health in this letter?
quiz.answer: He asks whether global health can recover its lost radicalism.

ai.caveat: This is a short editorial letter offering opinion and historical context, not a research study with data.

items.title: Evaluating an AI-Powered Patient Simulator for Communication Skills Training: One-Year Randomized Controlled Trial.

ai.headline: AI patient simulators may help medical students practise communication, but did not outperform conventional training in this trial.
ai.summary: A UK randomised trial followed 50 medical students for one academic year. Those using an AI-powered patient simulator improved descriptively more than controls, but the difference was not statistically significant; gains were linked to motivation and behavioural engagement.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that digital practice tools can support learning communication skills, but they are not yet proven to beat standard teaching.
ai.life_skill: Try practising difficult conversations regularly, whether with a person or a simulated tool, and notice what keeps you motivated to keep going.
ai.fact: In this trial, students’ communication skills improved over one academic year, and greater intrinsic motivation and behavioural learning were linked to larger gains.

quiz.question: Did the AI simulator group show a statistically significant improvement over conventional training?
quiz.answer: No, the AI group improved descriptively more, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant.

ai.caveat: The trial was small, non-blinded, and the AI-group advantage did not reach statistical significance, so the result should be treated as preliminary rather than proof.

items.title: Mental health of migrants in South Asia: a scoping review
items.venue: International Journal of Migration Health and Social Care

ai.headline: A review of 80 studies links migration in South Asia to depression, anxiety and PTSD, with trauma, poverty and isolation as key risks.
ai.summary: Researchers reviewed 80 peer-reviewed studies on migrant mental health in South Asia. Depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder were commonly studied, especially among refugees, displaced people and labour migrants. Violence, economic hardship, social isolation and discrimination were linked to poorer mental health, while family support, cultural practices and community resilience were protective.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how migration-related stress can affect mental wellbeing and highlights groups whose needs are often overlooked.
ai.life_skill: Notice if you or someone you know feels isolated or overwhelmed after moving, and consider reaching out to family, community or a qualified professional for support.
ai.fact: Family support, cultural practices and community resilience were identified as protective factors for migrant mental health in South Asia.

quiz.question: Which mental health issues were commonly studied among migrants in South Asia?
quiz.answer: Depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder were commonly studied.

ai.caveat: Most included studies were cross-sectional, so they show links rather than proving causes.

items.title: Context-driven mHealth solutions to improve maternal healthcare uptake in Ethiopia: Integrating stakeholder preferences and expert priorities using qualitative and nominal group techniques

ai.headline: Ethiopian women and experts agree on mobile health tools to improve maternal care uptake.
ai.summary: Researchers interviewed 72 perinatal women, male partners and key informants and held a workshop with 14 experts in Ethiopia. Participants preferred educational videos, text reminders followed by calls, involving spouses or support persons, and reminders sent between sunrise and midday the day before appointments.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how mobile health services can be shaped around local preferences and practical barriers to help more women attend pregnancy and postnatal care.
ai.life_skill: Notice what practical barriers, such as device access or network coverage, might stop a digital service from working in your community.
ai.fact: Only about one-quarter of women in Ethiopia complete the full continuum of maternal healthcare.
ai.caveat: This is a small qualitative and consensus study in one setting, so its findings are not proof that these interventions will work everywhere or improve health outcomes.

items.title: A Multimodal Study of Screen Use in Adolescents Across Brain Structure, Social Media, and Gaming Use

ai.headline: Problematic social media and gaming use are more strongly linked to adolescent attention problems than hours of screen time alone.
ai.summary: Researchers looked at over 11,000 adolescents and compared screen time, problematic social media use and problematic gaming with parent-rated mental health and brain measures. Problematic use scales were more strongly related to attention problems than hours of use, and more screen time was linked to slightly smaller putamen and caudate volumes.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests that how difficult a young person finds it to control their screen use may matter more for attention than the number of hours spent online.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether you struggle to stop using social media or games, rather than only counting screen hours.
ai.fact: More screen time was associated with slightly smaller putamen and caudate volumes in adolescents.

quiz.question: Which was more strongly related to attention problems: hours of screen time or problematic use scales?
quiz.answer: The problematic social media and gaming use scales were more strongly related to attention problems than hours of use were.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and the findings are observational so they cannot show that screen use causes attention problems or brain changes.

items.title: Spanish translation, cross-cultural adaptation, and psychometric validation of the CATQ-S and FATQ-S: assessing motivational functions of online and face-to-face aggression in secondary school students

ai.headline: Spanish questionnaires measuring why teenagers act aggressively online and face-to-face were validated for use in schools.
ai.summary: Researchers translated and culturally adapted two short questionnaires about the motivational functions of cyber and face-to-face aggression for Spanish secondary school students. Testing with 1,443 students aged 11–16 found the tools generally work well for boys and girls, though some aggression motives overlap too much to be clearly separated.
ai.why_it_matters: It gives schools and researchers a way to understand what drives peer aggression, which can inform efforts to support students’ wellbeing and safety.
ai.life_skill: Notice what might be driving aggressive behaviour—online or in person—before reacting.
ai.fact: The study involved 1,443 compulsory secondary education students from public schools in Extremadura, Spain.

quiz.question: What did the researchers validate for Spanish secondary school students?
quiz.answer: Short Spanish versions of questionnaires assessing motivational functions of cyber and face-to-face aggression.

ai.caveat: This was a single cross-sectional study in one Spanish region, so it shows the questionnaires work in that context but does not prove they reduce aggression or apply everywhere.

items.title: Latent profile analysis of ecological literacy among Turkish parents: associations with sociodemographic characteristics

ai.headline: Turkish parents’ ecological literacy awareness was modest overall, with education and family size linked to profile groups.
ai.summary: Researchers surveyed 543 parents in Türkiye about environmental values and everyday practices. Awareness scores were modest overall and did not differ by sociodemographic characteristics, but three distinct profiles emerged, with education level and number of children weakly linked to profile membership.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that parents’ environmental values may not match their everyday actions, which matters because parents shape children’s understanding of environmental issues.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether your everyday habits match your stated environmental values.
ai.fact: Ecological literacy includes both environmental values and their expression in everyday practices.

quiz.question: Did total ecological literacy scores differ across sociodemographic characteristics?
quiz.answer: No, total scores did not differ significantly across any characteristic examined.

ai.caveat: It used a convenience sample and self-reported awareness, so the results cannot prove cause and effect or apply beyond this group of parents in Türkiye.
